Crown squirrelfish (Sargocentron diadema) is a reef-associated holocentrid common throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. Following yolk-sac resorption, the onset of exogenous feeding marks a critical transition, after which the growing juvenile begins a phase of rapid mass gain. Field surveys of reef habitats throughout the Ryukyu Archipelago suggest that juvenile mortality is high during the initial weeks of benthic settlement, a pattern common among small-bodied reef fishes with pelagic larval durations. The rapid growth during the early larval stages is fueled by endogenous yolk reserves, and the transition to feeding on planktonic organisms marks a critical bottleneck for survival under field conditions.

As individuals progress through the sub-adult phase, the attainment of reproductive maturity is closely tied to body size rather than strictly to chronological age. Gonadal recrudescence in this species is likely cued by seasonal temperature cycles and photoperiod, ensuring that reproductive efforts coincide with periods of optimal planktonic food availability for the resulting larvae.

This lifespan is relatively extended for a fish of its maximum adult size, and it suggests a life-history strategy that balances early reproductive output with the potential for multiple spawning seasons across several years. The ultimate total length attained by this species is 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], and at this size a fully grown adult reaches an ultimate wet weight of 75.3 grams [Wwi = 75.3 grams] according to fitted length-weight regressions derived from extensive field collections across Micronesia. These asymptotic dimensions place Sargocentron diadema among the smaller members of the genus, yet its abundance on shallow forereefs indicates it occupies a well-defined trophic niche as a nocturnal plankton feeder with a moderate metabolic demand.

The relatively high fecundity at small body size suggests a compensatory life-history strategy that maximizes lifetime reproductive success despite high rates of egg and larval mortality typical of coral reef environments.
